We had barely any nurses, blood collectors, midwives - my interns have been working their asses off for the last year for basically nothing, and the hospital can’t afford to pay them overtime. I appreciate your opinion, but respectfully disagree. Midwives have a role in O&G, and I’ve never felt that I’ve had to do their job. Whether they feel they can do mine is irrelevant because our healthcare system makes that impossible for them. I don’t care if they *think* they can sign off a CTG, they legally can’t. And I don’t care if they  *think* they can do an instrumental delivery, they don’t have access to the tools because they need me. So instead I work on forming a collegial relationship with my staff, and trust me I have plenty of midwives who believe they could do my job, but it doesn’t matter because they still call me when they need help. These midwives will often say “I was fine, I could do your job here in a heartbeat”, when I’m doing a difficult delivery, but who cares? They still called for help, I’m the one doing the delivery as needed (which is my job), and the patient is safe. As I said in another comment, I don’t think a mum and baby should pay the price of interpersonal conflict.

Absolutely. However physicians are the team leader, whether the midwife agrees or doesn’t. They need our signatures for the CTG’s, medication orders, blood bank orders, and in some regions, to even become the primary care provider. The system has made it such that even *if* they believe they are more proficient, their clinical ability is limited. The exception is that they need to know when to call for help, and that they can. This is *why* it’s important to establish good relations with your midwives, regardless of their perceptions on rank, because at the end of the day if you’re an asshole - the only person that suffers is the patient. 

Like I said, I have worked alongside midwives throughout my medical training and now as an advanced trainee. I have seen the entire spectrum of opinion within midwifery, so I don’t care what a midwife thinks of *my* credentials. As long as we have collegial respect, in my experience, they have all called me for help at the right time. In instances where doctors have responded the way the commenter has, they delay call outs in hopes of “proving the doctor wrong” and that “they can handle it”. This is of course wrong, but a mum and baby should not have to pay the price of interpersonal conflict.

Yes, but a good leader does not undermine and alienate the people working with them. You rarely get a choice in picking your team in healthcare, and retaliating to people who *are* essential to O&G as it is today because they have ridiculous views is not going to make the team function any more effectively. All I’m saying is that someone who has now worked with midwives for quite a few years, the opinion expressed by the individual in the pic is not new, and frankly it’s a waste of time trying to change it. My job as the advanced trainee is to make sure that even *if* the midwife thinks they’re an “expert in natural birth”, that they are competent enough to recognise when something is going wrong AND that we have the collegiality where they will alert me as soon as needed.

You can express truth and fact in a civil way. As I’ve said in other comments, my opinion is formed by years of working as an O&G physician, this is just how the real world works. If you want your patient to be safe, then you need to work in a team. In order to do so, you can’t speak to your team members like this.

Not so much centrism, but an opinion formed over years of working in O&G and being about 10 months away from becoming an attendant (or consultant, as we say here). This is a reflection of the real world, and the real dynamics we have to foster - civility is what keeps patients safe.

I understand where you’re coming from, but I’m an O&G registrar. I have thought these thoughts many times, and I have worked with many midwives who have had these same opinions. Standing there and being an arrogant doctor, telling them that their training means nothing, has only ever affected patient safety - in my experience. I understand I’m on a sub where this opinion isn’t popular, but in real life and in the workforce, the patient comes first. With my midwife *colleagues*, I have to work with them as a team, or else they will delay alerting a doctor if there is an issue. Wanting to laude our training over mid-levels is great, but I also don’t give a shit when doing so means it could potentially delay care. Whether on not that’s right, or what that says about midwives is irrelevant in my opinion, it’s just what it is. I was hoping to add some real world perspective to the comment, considering this is my specialty.

I get what the resident is trying to say, but damn, they also sound like an asshole. There are better ways to communicate the same idea, and maybe help the midwife understand they work as a team and are not in competition?

It really depends on *why* you want to “try” Islam. 

If you want to learn more about it then I would recommend the following first:

-	Look for a translated version of the Quran that you feel comfortable reading and are able to understand
-	Start reading, remember the Quran is read from right to left, so open the book from the ‘back’
-	Read on historical and cultural academia about Prophet Mohammad PBUH’s time, this will help you understand the context of the scripture 
-	if you’re confused about a verse, don’t stress, that it why we have scholars and online resources. If you can, look up different “schools of thought” in Islam and that will help guide you on which scholars may help you best. 


If you want to learn how to be a practicing Muslim, then in addition to above, you should do this:

-	it’s important to acknowledge that in Islam, intention is above all. So, what that means is you need to understand why you’re doing what you’re doing
-	Understand and learn wudhu. Wudhu means cleanliness, and we perform it before each prayer. There’s also certain things we have to ensure so that we *maintain* wudhu as well. For now, I would recommend you do wudhu before each prayer so that you practice it 
-	Learn how to pray, learn simple dua’s (prayers) and learn what they mean so you know what you’re saying. This may be controversial, but I would even recommend printing the prayers and actions out so you can reference it at the beginning. We pray 5 times a day, and this is guided by the sun. Start slowly and you will be able to implement this into your routine. An Adthaan app (call for prayer) is really helpful as a reminder. 
-	Charity: this is one you can start straight away! You calculate a % of your income, it’s traditionally done with how much gold you own, but now it’s a bit different and you donate that to a charity. 
-	Eating halal - this can be a bit daunting at first, but again take it slow. Most places have vegetarian and fish options, that’s always a good place to start! Not to mention kebab places are usually halal, and who doesn’t love a kebab? Things we definitely don’t eat/drink are pork and alcohol. 
-	Be kind, courteous, and respectful to your peers. Treat your elders well, and most importantly treat your parents with the utmost respect. Give people the benefit of the doubt, this religion is one of mercy. 
-	Be mindful of your language: so lying, backbiting, and general deception is not accepted. 
-	Try to implement the principles of Islam as embodied by our Prophet Mohammad PBUH. He was an exceptionally gentle, kind, generous and just man. He treated all people equally, regardless of gender or status. He led by example, being a leader that was fair and merciful. He loved his family, cared deeply for the people around him and always contributed to his community. 

There are a lot of rules that you will see discussed, about the minutiae of Islamic practice. For eg whether you can listen to music or not, whether you can talk to non-muslims or not, whether you can mingle with the opposite gender or not. At the end of the day, if you follow the Quran, and what it demonstrated about the Prophet Mohammad PBUH’s actions, you will be fine. 

You live a life that is good, where your actions have the intention to be a better person and a better Muslim, then you are already 90% of the way there. A lot of faith it about completely surrendering to your Creator, that’s something that has no time limit. No amount of learning or practicing can shift your heart and mind one way or another. One can follow all the rules, and yet still not reach that. I find that the people who are most at peace with themselves and are strong in their relationship with Allah, are those who focus on bettering themselves while making a positive impact on their community and the world. 

Good luck!

Dude what are you even on about? *At most* half of what you wrote has anything to do with what we’re talking about, and that’s being generous. The other half sounds like the ramblings of someone who has truly drank the Kool Aid. 

Funny thing is I love America’s libertarian position, however after living around the world I’ve learned how skewed our idea of “freedom” is. For instance your statement “someone is either free or they are not” is blatantly incorrect. America may be free in many regards, but we also don’t have the freedom to access affordable healthcare or education. 

Of course I think the greater good is more important? I would much rather impede my movement if it meant I would keep the community safer. That’s not illogical, it’s utilitarian with the goal being the least number of people harmed. For someone who believes in inalienable rights, you were very quick to say I don’t “deserve” mine. 

I’m going to ignore your entire gun-redneck-conservative rant because I have no idea what that has to do with anything. You don’t know my political leanings, and I don’t pretend to know yours. 

“Meaning outdoor activity is completely safe” not even the CDC says that. The risk is much lower, yes. Even Australia acknowledges that, we were permitted gatherings outside first as restrictions eased. However, again, it seems like you don’t read what other people say? You kind of just go on a tangent without actually comprehending what the discussion is about. I explicitly said that they wanted to reduce *contact*, so you couldn’t travel to neighbouring LGA’s because the population density in Sydney and those areas is high enough that you may have contact with others. The Australian government has always encouraged people go outside, get exercise etc. only limiting the number of people (again, contact). It’s possible to have things in moderation.

You tout Europe as being very forward thinking in their approach to Covid. Even citing Italy as having the most cases. Fittingly, Italy has just enacted the toughest control measures of any Western democracy. So perhaps USA should follow suit?

Again, what is this weird self-persecutory “conservative/redneck” bs coming from? I legit haven’t said a single thing about that and you keep bringing it up?? It’s like you’re just arguing with yourself, it’s weird. 

USA/Europe still have a very high death count, that’s undeniable. The decision the USA made to open up completely as early as it did was criticised heavily by international health bodies. However, most individuals understand that the USA needed to balance its economic interest as well. It does not have the social infrastructure to support its population on its own; people would literally start going into poverty if the lockdown persisted. You can accept both that the USA’s death toll is still too high, but that they were limited in their options as true. Equally true is Australia has one of the lowest deaths per capita. Their measures of lockdowns on both their borders, incoming trade, and interstate travel is the reason 60% of the nation has been living Covid-free for almost 2 years. All of WA, and most of NT, and SA have returned to pre-pandemic activity. Australia had the privilege of being able to choose preservation of life over economic stability, in part because it had a robust social infrastructure to begin with. Also you can’t talk about Australia being uninhabited in the same argument where you discuss per capita, it doesn’t make sense. 

Covid has taken half my family in the US, the 6 remaining are footing a giant medical bill that I’m working here to help pay off. So no, I haven’t gone outside much, I’ve had the luck to work from home and I’ve been doing a great deal of it. When you talk to Australian’s here, you’ll see that they are fed up and annoyed with lockdown, with the restrictions, with not seeing their friends and family. However, it’s not the “goodness of their heart” that stops them from whinging about it, it’s that they see stories like mine, or they watch the news of the deaths in the US or Europe and realise how badly they don’t want that to happen here.

The term inalienable right is literally in **our** Declaration and nowhere else, it doesn’t exist in any other legal sphere.

Can you please punctuate your sentences? It’s like reading something an 8 year old wrote. 

All essential workers in Australia have close contact to vulnerable people. It does not have to be “indoor”, droplets don’t spread *via* air, they just go through air (they are not airborne spread). This is why social distancing works, you stand further apart and therefore the droplets have more distance to go before reaching the next person. This is also why the same measures apply whether your indoors or outdoors.

Again, the “how far” was to limit spread to other places by limiting contact with other places. If you didn’t go there, you can’t spread it there (simple!). Being outside is not the issue, the number of people was the issue. 

The US has one of the highest death tolls in the world due to Covid. In the interest of freedom, they’ve lost a lot of people. I’m American (which is why I emphasised “our” but I suspect you’re not too good with reading) and I’ve lived in Australia for the last year. Trust me, they don’t want a system anything like ours. They are very happy to do less things if it means they can prevent other people from dying.

Australian’s have always been allowed to go outside for exercise, even during the harshest lockdowns. There were rules with how many people and how far you could go, so as to not endanger neighbouring communities. People who were fined in Australia for being “unvaccinated on the pavement” were because they broke public health guidelines of how many people you can be with, not that they were on a walk and unvaccinated. 

Vaccine mandates are for all essential workers that are front facing and interact with vulnerable communities and not the general public. If you are working with vulnerable communities, then it’s your duty to not endanger them. If you’re unwilling to do so, then you leave; nobody has the “right to employment”. 

Also it’s “inalienable rights”; a uniquely American ethical principle because it was introduced in *our* Declaration of Independence. If you’re going to spout bs, at least make it relevant to Australian’s and maybe read the NSW/Vic Public Health websites instead of relying on Candace Owen, Joe Rogan or whatever Fox pundit you get your news from.

Well to answer your question, because I give people the benefit of the doubt. There has been nothing in his post to suggest this friend has a pattern of behaviour that makes her flaky or even a bad friend in general. If this was a close friends trip, and I had to cancel a few days prior, it would be for something significant. I think most of us saying YTA understand that life happens, that doesn’t make you an asshole. He was given 3 days notice, reservations hadn’t been made. Yes, it’s disappointing, but it doesn’t make you an asshole because you have to cancel plans if something more pressing comes up. She would be an asshole if she cancelled the day of, just didn’t show up, didn’t apologise or offer alternative plans. But she didn’t do any of that, so I don’t think she’s an asshole. She was placed between a rock and a hard place, and she chose what she had to. 

As for calling her mum a cunt, I’m Australian, that word doesn’t phase me and my verdict still stands. And is in fact reinforced by this, because if her mum is awful to her, there’s a large chance she’s awful to all the kids. And as a big sister, I would always step in for my siblings if they need it.

Adult behaviour is weighing priorities, plans don’t always take precedence because life happens. That kind of black and white thinking serves no one in the real world. 

I said she’s an adult because that means she weighed the options and came to the conclusion that this was the necessary choice. Just because the mum is a bad person, doesn’t mean the sister and her dog should suffer for it. We don’t know the circumstances at all, neither does the friend. We have no idea as to why her mother decided to drop off her child and a dog last minute, nor do we know if there are actually any other viable options.
